name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,865

clue.text: Monsieur enters to have a little soup (8)

indicators.note: Someone who enters a room ends up inside it, so the letter arrives in the middle of the word beside it rather than alongside.

blocks.note: to have someone, in the sense of tricking them, is to con them
M is the standard abbreviation for the French courtesy title, as written on an envelope
a little of something is some of it, and the Frenchman's letter goes in among these four

annotation.walkthrough: 'to have' looks like joinery holding the sentence up; it is the first chunk of the wordplay, in the sense of having someone over.
annotation.definitionFit: soup -> CONSOMME: a clear broth simmered from meat stock and served as a first course, so the general word names one particular dish.

clue.text: Bit of wind taking the wings off two Boeings (4)

indicators.note: Wings are the outer edges of a thing, so stripping them leaves only what was sitting in the middle of the words.

blocks.note: four consecutive letters run across the join between these two words once the outer ones are gone

annotation.walkthrough: Boeing builds aeroplanes, so 'wings' reads as part of the picture rather than as an instruction. The aircraft never matter; only the spelling does.
annotation.definitionFit: Bit of wind -> OBOE: an instrument sounded by blowing, so it belongs to the wind section of an orchestra and 'bit of' picks out one member.

clue.text: Son worked on boat up the creek (7)

blocks.note: S is the standard abbreviation for son, as on a family tree
the hands who work a boat are its crew, and as a verb they crewed her

annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a lad helping out on the water. 'Up the creek' is the short form of being up it without a paddle, which is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: up the creek -> SCREWED: both are idioms for being stuck in hopeless trouble with no way out, the answer being the blunter modern one.

clue.text: Rug on top for Spooner? Surely not (2,3)

indicators.note: The Reverend Spooner was famous for trading the opening sounds of two words, so the phrase clued has to be said with its first sounds swapped.

blocks.note: whatever sits on top of everything else is high up
a mat is a small rug, the sort you wipe your feet on
the two pieces stand as HIGH MAT, and trading their opening sounds gives what you write in

annotation.walkthrough: A Spoonerism happens in the mouth, not on paper: say the two words with their first sounds exchanged and out comes an old-fashioned cry of disbelief.
annotation.definitionFit: Surely not -> MY HAT: 'my hat!' is a dated British exclamation of flat disbelief, registering the same refusal to accept what has just been claimed.

clue.text: Shortened horsy draught animal's 12 hour day (7)

indicators.note: A shortened word has lost its tail, so the adjective beside it is written without its final letter.

blocks.note: horsy is equine in a vet's vocabulary, and the word arrives with its last letter clipped
an ox is the beast harnessed to pull a plough or a cart

annotation.walkthrough: The definition is exact rather than loose: on this date daylight and darkness each last twelve hours, which happens twice a year.
annotation.definitionFit: 12 hour day -> EQUINOX: the date when the sun crosses the equator and light and dark come out equal, twelve hours apiece.

clue.text: Really enjoy Alien in which ship's beginning to dissolve with acid (6)

indicators.note: The clue says the vessel's letter is in the creature, so that letter is planted between its two rather than added on the end.
A word's beginning is the letter it opens with, so only that one is taken from the vessel.

blocks.note: to dig something, in sixties slang, is to be very keen on it
ET is the crossword's standard alien, short for extraterrestrial
the first letter of ship, the vessel the surface has in mind

annotation.walkthrough: Italics mark Alien as the film, which is scene-setting only. The wordplay wants the two-letter alien every crossword uses, and a spacecraft is just a ship.
annotation.definitionFit: dissolve with acid -> DIGEST: the stomach breaks food down in acid, and that is precisely the process this verb names.

clue.text: Scoffing expert finally said "That is an old master" (9)

indicators.note: Finally points at the end of the word beside it, so only its closing letter is taken.

blocks.note: the closing letter of said
i.e. is short for the Latin id est, which translates as that is
Titian was the great Venetian painter of the sixteenth century, one of the old masters

annotation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make the last five words sound like someone admiring a painting on a wall; the wordplay reads them piece by piece instead.
annotation.definitionFit: Scoffing expert -> DIETITIAN: scoff is British slang for eating greedily, so the scoffing expert is the professional who advises on what people eat.

clue.text: Burning light alarmingly close in space (3,4)

indicators.note: A thing said to be in another sits among its letters, so the piece just clued is dropped into the middle of the one that follows.

blocks.note: a gap is the space left between two things
to slam a door is to close it hard enough to make everyone jump

annotation.walkthrough: The surface pictures two objects nearly colliding out in the cosmos. 'Close' is not a distance at all but a door being shut, and 'space' is only a gap.
annotation.definitionFit: Burning light -> GAS LAMP: a lamp with a live flame inside it, so unlike a bulb this kind of light really is burning.

clue.text: Acting independently troubled Nelson a tad (5-5)

indicators.note: Troubled water is churned up and no longer settled, so the letters beside the word will not stay in the order they are given.

blocks.note: these ten letters, shaken out of the order the clue prints them in

annotation.walkthrough: Nelson lends the surface an admiral who stops mattering the moment you count: the name and 'a tad' hold exactly ten letters, which is the enumeration.
annotation.definitionFit: Acting independently -> STAND-ALONE: a stand-alone unit works on its own without being plugged into anything else, which is independence described as equipment.

clue.text: Trying venue where race might be held that accommodates 1,000 (10)

indicators.note: To accommodate guests is to house them within your walls, so the number named next goes inside the letters already clued.

blocks.note: a race is run over a course, whether the runners are horses or people
thou is the everyday short form of a thousand

annotation.walkthrough: 'Trying' is the pun: not wearisome but conducting a trial. The surface keeps you at the racetrack, where the same word would mean a testing afternoon.
annotation.definitionFit: Trying venue -> COURTHOUSE: the building where trials are heard, so 'trying' is the legal verb at work rather than the tiring adjective.

clue.text: Anorak's over fleece (4)

indicators.note: Something turned over lies the other way round, so the letters just clued are read from the far end back.

blocks.note: an anorak is a mac, the British word for a raincoat, and one belonging to somebody makes MACS, written in the other way round

annotation.walkthrough: Both halves of the clue talk about coats: an anorak in the wordplay and a sheep's fleece in the definition, and only one of them is really clothing.
annotation.definitionFit: fleece -> SCAM: both are verbs for cheating a person out of their money, one drawn from shearing sheep and the other from confidence tricks.

clue.text: Wii boxing in back of tavern in Thailand, drunken comedy (8,3,1)

indicators.note: To box something in is to shut it on every side, so the console's letters close round everything else.
The back of a word is its final letter, so one letter comes out of the tavern and no more.
The country is where the tavern's letter is put, so it lands among the letters of the name rather than beside them.

blocks.note: Nintendo's games console, spelled with a double i
the letter at the back of the word tavern
the country supplies eight letters, opened up early on to take the tavern's letter

annotation.walkthrough: 'Drunken' looks like an instruction to shuffle and is not: it belongs to the definition, describing a 1987 film about two soaked out-of-work actors.
annotation.definitionFit: drunken comedy -> WITHNAIL AND I: Bruce Robinson's film follows two permanently sozzled actors through a wet weekend, so the definition names it by its plot.

clue.text: Get rid of husband, but shag single comedian first (2,4,4)

indicators.note: What comes first is written at the front, so the three pieces just clued line up ahead of the letter for the spouse.

blocks.note: to bed someone is the printable verb for what the surface says more coarsely
a single of anything is one of it
a wit is someone whose talk gets laughs, which is a comedian's whole trade
H is the standard abbreviation for husband, as on a form

annotation.walkthrough: The order is the trap: the husband is named at the start of the clue and written at the end of the answer, and 'but' only props the sentence up.
annotation.definitionFit: Get rid of -> BE DONE WITH: to be done with a person is to have finished with them for good, which is disposal put as a decision.

clue.text: Sponge without water perhaps upsetting Mary, die on cross (5-3)

indicators.note: To upset a tray is to tip everything on it into a heap, and letters tipped over land in a different order.

blocks.note: seven letters tipped out of their printed order
a cross is written as an X, the mark on a ballot paper

annotation.walkthrough: The definition is a packet of dry cake mix: add water and you get a sponge. 'Perhaps' is there because concrete is sold the same way.
annotation.definitionFit: Sponge without water perhaps -> READY-MIX: the packet holds everything a sponge needs except the liquid, so the cake is one example of what comes premixed.

clue.text: You must cut extremely long hair (9)

indicators.note: To cut into something is to go right through the middle of it, so the letter for the reader lands inside the word that follows.

blocks.note: extremely rich and most rich say the same thing, so the adverb hands over four letters
U stands in for you in text-message spelling
to long for something is to ache for it

annotation.walkthrough: 'You must cut' reads as an order barked at the solver, and that is exactly what it is — an instruction about one letter, not about anybody's hair.
annotation.definitionFit: hair -> MOUSTACHE: the definition names the general stuff and the answer is one particular growth of it, the kind worn on the upper lip.

clue.text: Stick one's china back on mantelpiece (6)

indicators.note: The back of a word is its rear end, so what is wanted from the long one is the single letter it finishes on.

blocks.note: a person speaking of themselves turns one is into I'm, two letters once the apostrophe goes
china plate is Cockney rhyming slang for mate, and a mate is a pal
the letter this long word ends on

annotation.walkthrough: 'Stick' is the definition and it is a verb, meaning to run something through on a spike — not the noun the ornaments and the mantelpiece invite.
annotation.definitionFit: Stick -> IMPALE: to stick a fork through a piece of meat is to impale it, the verb for driving a point clean through something.

clue.text: Japanese island ducks largely avoid (6)

indicators.note: Largely means most of a thing but not all of it, so the word beside it arrives with its final letter missing.

blocks.note: ducks is a British term of address for someone you are fond of, and hon, short for honey, does the same job
to avoid a person is to shun them, and the word turns up here a letter short

annotation.walkthrough: 'Ducks' looks like waterfowl, or a batter's score of nothing; it is the friendly Midlands form of address, the sort said across a shop counter.
annotation.definitionFit: Japanese island -> HONSHU: the largest of Japan's islands and the one holding Tokyo, so the definition names it by country and kind.

clue.text: Shoe reeks, case of aeration failing? (7)

indicators.note: A case is the shell that encloses a thing, so what is taken is the pair of letters at either end of the word.
Something failing is coming apart at the seams, and letters that come apart can be reassembled in any order.

blocks.note: the two letters that case this word, one at each end
five letters as printed, waiting to be reordered along with the pair beside them

annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the whole picture as invention: footwear has no aeration case. It is there so 'case of' reads as a complaint rather than an order.
annotation.definitionFit: Shoe -> SNEAKER: a soft rubber-soled trainer, named for how quietly you can creep about in it, so it is one kind of shoe.

clue.text: Accurately position leg and off-side fielder (8)

blocks.note: pins is old slang for legs, as in being unsteady on them
point is the cricket fielding position square of the batter on the off side

annotation.walkthrough: Cricket divides the field into the leg side and the off side, and the clue uses both words — one as a limb, one as a genuine fielding position.
annotation.definitionFit: Accurately position -> PINPOINT: to pinpoint a target is to fix exactly where it is, the verb borrowed from marking a map with a pin.

clue.text: Half retire in style earlier than expected (7)

indicators.note: Half of a six-letter word is three letters, and the front half is what the clue hands over.
A piece described as being in another is planted among its letters rather than added at either end.

blocks.note: a perm is a hairstyle, short for permanent wave
the first half of retire, three of its six letters

annotation.walkthrough: 'Half retire' is solver's shorthand for taking half the letters, not for going part-time, and the early retirement in the surface is the joke.
annotation.definitionFit: earlier than expected -> PRETERM: a preterm baby arrives before its due date, the prefix pre- carrying exactly that sense of ahead of time.

clue.text: How to serve cheese and beans? Not with head inside oven (2,5)

definitions.text: How to serve cheese and beans

indicators.note: What goes inside a word sits between its letters, so the letter just named moves into the middle of what is left of it.

blocks.note: the word Not with its leading letter taken away
the head of a word is the letter at its front, here the one just removed
an oast is the kiln in a Kentish oast house, built for drying hops

annotation.walkthrough: The trick is that the letter taken off the front never leaves the clue: it moves back in one place, which is why the letter count never changes.
annotation.definitionFit: How to serve cheese and beans -> ON TOAST: both are British teatime staples ladled over a hot slice, so the phrase answers what they sit on.

clue.text: Old record tied yet broken in prospect (7-5)

indicators.note: A broken thing is in pieces that can be put back any way round, so the three letters beside the word are reordered.
Something in a thing lies within its letters, so the pieces assembled first are planted inside the word that follows.

blocks.note: a prospect is a view, and a view is a sight
scores that are tied are level, or even
the three letters of yet, put back in another order

annotation.walkthrough: 'Record ... broken' is the surface's athletics story and has nothing to do with it: the record here is the brittle shellac disc a wind-up gramophone played.
annotation.definitionFit: Old record -> SEVENTY-EIGHT: shellac discs are named after the revolutions a minute they spin at, and collectors still call them by that number.

clue.text: Put precious coat on to cover uniform for society (5)

indicators.note: To cover something is to lie over it on both sides, so the letter named next is taken in among the ones already clued.

blocks.note: to gild is to lay a thin skin of gold over something
U is uniform in the radio alphabet, where every letter has a spoken name

annotation.walkthrough: 'Put precious coat on' is one instruction rather than three, and 'precious' is in it only because the metal being laid on has to be gold.
annotation.definitionFit: society -> GUILD: an association of craftsmen banded together to protect a trade, so it is one particular kind of society.

clue.text: Slow mover missing the last scheduled time (4)

indicators.note: Missing the last means the final letter has gone, so the creature's name is written out one letter short.

blocks.note: the sloth hangs about in South American trees and is a byword for going nowhere fast

annotation.walkthrough: The surface grumbles about a dawdler who has missed the last bus. 'The last' is not part of that story: it is an instruction about a letter.
annotation.definitionFit: scheduled time -> SLOT: the fixed gap in a timetable that a plane or a broadcast is allotted, so it names a booked stretch of time.

clue.text: Beat little pest that won't let go (4)

definitions.text: little pest that won't let go

blocks.note: a clock marks each beat of time with one small sound

blocks.clueFragment: little pest that won't let go
blocks.note: the parasite that buries its head in a dog's skin and cannot be shaken off

annotation.walkthrough: Nothing is anagrammed or hidden here: the clue simply sets two unrelated meanings side by side and lets the surface pretend they are one sentence.
annotation.definitionFit: Beat -> TICK: the regular beat of a clock, while the little pest is the blood-sucking mite that fastens onto skin and holds until pulled off.

clue.text: Decent plastic ID bracelet (10)

indicators.note: Plastic means easily moulded into another shape, so the letters beside the word can be pressed into a different order.

blocks.note: the ten letters of these two words, pressed into a new shape

annotation.walkthrough: 'Plastic ID bracelet' is one believable object, which is what hides the instruction inside it. The enumeration is the tell: the phrase holds exactly ten letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Decent -> CREDITABLE: work that does you credit is respectable enough to earn praise, which is what calling a performance decent amounts to.

clue.text: Bill right to replace note in coins (6)

indicators.note: Replacing means one letter steps out and another steps into the same spot, so the word keeps the length it started with.

blocks.note: the coins rattling in your pocket are your change
N is the standard abbreviation for note, and it is the letter that leaves
R is the standard abbreviation for right, as on a diagram

annotation.walkthrough: 'Bill', 'note' and 'coins' are all money on the surface, which is the misdirection: two of them are money and the third is a single letter.
annotation.definitionFit: Bill -> CHARGE: the sum a garage or a restaurant charges you is what turns up on the bill, so both name the amount demanded.

clue.text: Consider change to clue, perhaps Mike worried about it? (8)

indicators.note: About means around, and 'it' points back at the alteration just clued, so the two short pieces close round that word.

blocks.note: Mike is M in the radio alphabet, the same list that gives uniform for U
changing a piece of writing is editing it, and a clue is one example of writing
what worried you ate at you, in the idiom about something eating a person

annotation.walkthrough: The question mark covers 'perhaps': a clue is only one example of the thing being changed. On the surface a setter is fretting over his own puzzle.
annotation.definitionFit: Consider -> MEDITATE: to meditate on a problem is to turn it over in the mind at length, which is considering it slowly and deliberately.
